author: reek
body: "RSD PTR " -- eight bytes, the trailing space included.

author: reek
body: Interrupt controller structures start at offset 44, each a (type, length) pair. Type 1 is an I/O APIC, whose 32-bit address sits at offset 4 within the structure. Type 5 overrides the local APIC address with a 64-bit value and, when present, wins over the 32-bit field at MADT offset 36. A zero length would not advance the walk, so we stop.

author: reek
body: To power the machine off an OS writes the sleep type the firmware chose, not a number it guessed. That number lives in the DSDT as Name (_S5_, Package () { SLP_TYPa, SLP_TYPb, ... }), encoded in AML. This is a targeted scan, not an AML interpreter: find the four bytes "_S5_", require a PackageOp immediately after, skip the package length and the element count, and decode the first two elements.

author: reek
body: The element cursor: past "_S5_" (4) and PackageOp (1) sits the package length byte, then that many extra length bytes, then NumElements.

author: reek
body: A revision 2 RSDP must satisfy both checksums: the first twenty bytes for the benefit of a 1.0 reader, and the whole declared length.

author: reek
body: If the write lands, execution never reaches here. If the firmware declined the transition, spin rather than fall off the end of the world into whatever bytes follow.

author: val
body: ACPI table discovery for the Option A boot path (H1b). Until now the payload assumed the LAPIC at 0xFEE00000 and the IOAPIC at 0xFEC00000 and had no idea how to power the machine off -- a hardcoded gamble that happens to hold on the boards we have tried. The firmware knows the real answers and publishes them in the ACPI tables; the boot stub captures the RSDP pointer from the UEFI configuration table (the RSDP is a vendor table, not a protocol, so LocateProtocol cannot find it) and leaves it in a cell. Everything here reads from that pointer.

author: val
body: Two shapes must both work. An ACPI 1.0 RSDP (revision 0) offers only a 32-bit RsdtAddress, and the RSDT's entries are 32-bit. An ACPI 2.0+ RSDP (revision 2 and up) also offers a 64-bit XsdtAddress whose entries are 64-bit; we prefer it. codex-vm publishes both. Real firmware on any machine made this century publishes both.

author: val
body: Assembled from bytes rather than taken from peek-32, because a table field like the local APIC address (0xFEE00000) has bit 31 set and a sign-extending 32-bit load would report it as a negative number.

author: val
body: A conforming table's bytes sum to zero modulo 256. We verify the RSDP and the root table, whose lengths are small and known. We do not checksum the DSDT: on real firmware it runs to kilobytes of AML, and a bad byte there would surface as a failed _S5_ decode, which we handle.

author: val
body: The RSDT holds 32-bit pointers from offset 36; the XSDT holds 64-bit pointers from the same offset. Entry count follows from the header length. acpi-find returns the address of the first table whose signature matches, or 0.

author: val
body: Field offsets are the spec's, and they are not obvious: FIRMWARE_CTRL at 36 and DSDT at 40, then the power-management block addresses -- PM1a_EVT_BLK at 56 and PM1a_CNT_BLK at 64. Reading PM1a_CNT_BLK from the wrong offset yields the event block, and a shutdown written there does nothing. A revision 2 FADT (length past 148) carries a 64-bit X_DSDT at 140 that supersedes the 32-bit field.

author: val
body: A revision 2 FADT (length 129 and up) may publish a reset register: flags bit 10 (RESET_REG_SUP) at offset 112 declares it, a Generic Address Structure at 116 names the register (address space id first, the 64-bit address at 120), and RESET_VALUE at 128 is the byte to write. A shorter FADT has no such fields and reading them would be reading the next table's bytes.

author: val
body: A package length's leading byte carries the count of following length bytes in its top two bits. Elements here are constants: ZeroOp (0x00) is 0, OneOp (0x01) is 1, and BytePrefix (0x0A) introduces a literal byte. Anything else means an encoding we do not read, and we decline.

author: val
body: The declared length is bounded before it is used as a loop count. The spec's RSDP is 36 bytes; a candidate found by scanning memory can carry any four bytes there, and a length of four billion would walk the whole address space inside a checksum.

author: val
body: The S5 transition: write the sleep type the firmware published, with SLP_EN set, to the PM1a control block. SLP_TYP occupies bits 10 to 12 and SLP_EN is bit 13, so the value is (SLP_TYPa << 10) | 0x2000. When the FADT names a PM1b control block the same is done there with SLP_TYPb; a machine with a split control block needs both halves.

author: val
body: We do not perform the legacy ACPI-enable handshake (write ACPI_ENABLE to SMI_CMD, then poll SCI_EN). UEFI firmware places the machine in ACPI mode before it hands control to a boot application, so the handshake belongs to the BIOS era, and issuing it blind would poke a port whose meaning we have not read. If a board ever needs it, the FADT already tells us its SMI_CMD and ACPI_ENABLE.

author: val
body: acpi-poweroff refuses rather than guesses: without a parsed FADT, a decoded _S5_, and a control-block address, it returns -1 and the machine stays on. A caller that gets -1 has learned something true about the firmware.

author: val
body: Warm reset, by preference order. The FADT's reset register is the firmware's own answer and is honored when declared: a byte written to an I/O port or a memory address, whichever the Generic Address Structure names. The 0xCF9 reset-control port is the universal PC chipset fallback (bit 1 selects a hard reset, bit 2 pulses it). The i8042 output-port pulse is last, and only when a status read shows a controller actually present -- 0xFF is the floating bus, and writing reset commands into it is theater. Unlike poweroff, reset never refuses: 0xCF9 exists on every PC-compatible chipset. If every write is somehow ignored, spin.

author: val
body: The Option A stub writes the RSDP pointer it found in the UEFI configuration table to cell 0x8028, beside the framebuffer handoff. Zero means the firmware exposed no ACPI table at all.

author: val
body: ACPI 6.5 section 5.2.5.1 gives the IA-PC search when nobody hands the pointer over: the first kilobyte of the Extended BIOS Data Area, then the BIOS read-only area 0xE0000 to 0xFFFFF, on 16-byte boundaries in both. The EBDA segment is the 16-bit word at 0x40E of the BIOS data area and addresses it in paragraphs, so it is shifted left four. A segment outside 0x80000 to 0xA0000 is not an EBDA, and on a machine whose firmware left that word alone it is whatever was in the RAM.

author: val
body: A payload reaches this only when nothing published a pointer, which is not the rare case it reads as: a plain CDX started on a bare -gop guest has no boot stub at all, and until now it reported a machine with no ACPI while the tables sat at 0xE0000 unread. The stub's pointer is still asked for first and still wins.
